question:
Patient note:
A 41-year-old woman is seen this afternoon in the ambulatory surgery holding area immediately before a planned right knee arthroscopy with partial meniscectomy and chondroplasty after two months of mechanical symptoms that have not responded to physiotherapy; the procedure is expected to last less than an hour under general anesthesia with a rapid recovery pathway. Three weeks ago, while descending a flight of stairs, she inverted her right foot and sustained a grade II ankle sprain that orthopedic clinic elected to treat with a fiberglass short-leg cast to control pain and minimize further ligamentous injury; plain radiographs obtained at that visit confirmed the absence of any hip, pelvic, or leg fracture. Since the cast application she has spent nearly all of each day propped on pillows in bed or on a couch, rising only with assistance to use the bathroom, and her activity tracker records fewer than 250 steps daily. She reports no other operations, endoscopic procedures, or invasive interventions during the preceding month and has not required emergency care or unplanned admissions. She has not experienced any episode of systemic infection, sepsis, pneumonia, or other acute cardiopulmonary illness during this period. The medical history is remarkable for a ten-year history of ileocolonic Crohn disease that is currently quiescent on adalimumab 40 mg every other week, last dose nine days ago, and oral mesalamine 2.4 g daily; she has never needed systemic corticosteroids, total parenteral nutrition, or surgical bowel resection. She has no history of congestive heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, stroke, transient ischemic attack, spinal cord injury, or multi-system trauma, and no prior thrombotic events have been documented. Cardiopulmonary review is negative for orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, sputum, dyspnea on exertion, wheeze, palpitations, exertional chest discomfort, presyncope, or pedal edema. She denies fevers, chills, sweats, rigors, productive sputum, or clinician-diagnosed pneumonia in recent weeks, and has not experienced erythema, warmth, or drainage around the ankle cast. There is no prior history of clots in the legs or lungs, and duplex ultrasonography performed five years ago for unilateral calf soreness during marathon training was normal; similarly, computed tomography of the chest has never demonstrated embolic disease. Neither parent nor her two sisters has had venous thrombosis or early cerebrovascular events, and there is no known hereditary thrombophilia among relatives. She has never received a peripherally inserted central catheter, infusion port, or tunneled dialysis catheter, and current venous access is a single 20-gauge peripheral line placed by nursing staff this morning. Medications aside from her Crohn regimen include over-the-counter vitamin D and calcium; she does not use estrogen-containing contraception, selective estrogen receptor modulators, antiplatelet agents, erythropoiesis-stimulating drugs, or chronic steroids. She quit smoking at age 30 after a 10-pack-year exposure and drinks wine twice monthly; illicit drug use is denied. On examination she lies supine with the head of bed elevated 20°, converses comfortably, and moves only her upper body because of lower-extremity discomfort from the cast. Vital signs: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 114/68 mm Hg, heart rate 72 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98 % on room air, body mass index 24 kg/m². Neck veins are not distended; the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced, S1 and S2 are crisp, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops are audible. Lungs are clear bilaterally with normal percussion and symmetric expansion. Abdomen is soft with well-healed laparoscopy port scars from a diagnostic procedure performed years earlier; there is no tenderness or hepatosplenomegaly. Inspection of the lower limbs shows an intact fiberglass cast extending from just below the tibial tubercle to the metatarsal heads, dry and odor-free; the contralateral leg reveals multiple tortuous, bluish superficial veins along the posteromedial calf that become more prominent on dangling, without overlying skin changes, focal calf tenderness, or pitting edema. Neither leg is swollen, and circumferential measurements above the malleoli are symmetric. Both feet are warm with brisk capillary refill, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses palpable 2+ and symmetric, and there is no palpable venous cord. Neurologic screening demonstrates intact cranial nerves, full upper-extremity strength, and normal sensation to light touch distal to the cast edges. Laboratory results drawn yesterday show hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, hematocrit 39 %, platelets 244 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 6.8 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 0.84 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 19 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.0 s with an international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. A resting electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min with normal intervals, and a chest radiograph obtained for pre-operative screening last week is clear. Airway assessment reveals Mallampati class II, full cervical range of motion, adequate thyromental distance, and intact dentition; anesthesia predicts easy mask ventilation and routine laryngoscopy. Sequential pneumatic compression sleeves have been ordered but are not yet applied, and no anticoagulant prophylaxis has been administered pending completion of surgical time-out and line placement.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini VTE score adds the points for each qualifying perioperative risk factor:
- Age 41–60 years: she is 41 (+1).
- Arthroscopic surgery: planned knee arthroscopy (+2). Do not also count minor surgery.
- Immobilizing plaster or fiberglass cast: short-leg cast (+2).
- Confinement to bed for more than 72 hours: three weeks with only assisted bathroom trips (+2).
- Visible varicose veins: tortuous superficial calf veins (+1).
- History of inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn disease (+1), even in remission.
The standard sum is 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 9. The subtotal is 8 only if a qualifying one-point factor, such as Crohn disease, is omitted.
Final answer: 8
